comparison: not gradable — extreme, it already means *very big*: *absolutely huge*, *really huge*; *huger* and *hugest* exist but are rare — say *much bigger* or *the biggest*
contrast: *Huge* already contains *very*, so *very huge* sounds like a learner: say *really huge*, *absolutely huge* or simply *very big*. *A huge fan* is someone who likes something a lot, not a large person.

senses.gloss: Extremely large in size, amount or degree.
examples: They live in a *huge* house outside Dallas.
The difference in price was *huge*.
Thanks — that's a *huge* help.

senses.gloss: Very popular, successful or important, informal.
examples: The band is still *huge* in Japan.
Podcasts got *huge* in just a few years.
Winning that contract is *huge* for a small company like ours.

comparison: -er/-est — *tinier*, *tiniest*
contrast: *Tiny* is the extreme of *small*, so it goes more naturally with *really* or *absolutely* than with *very*, though *very tiny* is heard in speech. Americans often double it for effect: *a tiny little dog*, *teeny-tiny*. The *y* changes to *i* before *-er* and *-est*: *tinier*, *tiniest*.

senses.gloss: Extremely small.
examples: They rented a *tiny* apartment in Manhattan.
The print on the label was *tiny*.
She noticed even the *tiniest* mistake.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely enormous*, not *very enormous*; *more enormous* is rare — say *even bigger*
contrast: Extreme, so not *very enormous*: say *absolutely enormous* or *really enormous*, and use the adverb *enormously* to intensify other words (*enormously popular*). The noun *enormity* is a trap: careful writers keep it for great wickedness (*the enormity of the crime*) and object to *the enormity of the task* when only size is meant.

senses.gloss: Extremely large in size, amount or degree.
examples: An *enormous* truck blocked the whole street.
The pressure on the team was *enormous*.
She's made an *enormous* difference at this school.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely gigantic*, not *very gigantic*
contrast: Extreme, so not *very gigantic*. *Giant* also works as an adjective, but only before a noun (*a giant step*, *giant waves*); after *be* use *gigantic* or *huge*: *The waves were gigantic*, not *The waves were giant*.

senses.gloss: Extremely large; much bigger than usual.
examples: A *gigantic* wave crashed over the pier.
The new mall is *gigantic*.
We ordered a *gigantic* pizza for the whole team.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun (*freezing rain*, *freezing temperatures*)
comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely freezing*, not *very freezing*
contrast: Extreme, so *It's absolutely freezing*, not *very freezing*. *I'm freezing* means I feel very cold; *frozen* food or a *frozen* lake has actually turned to ice. In *freezing cold* the word works like an adverb meaning *extremely* (*freezing cold water*). In the United States the freezing point in a forecast is 32°F.

senses.gloss: Extremely cold, of the weather, a place, water or a part of the body.
examples: It's *freezing* out there — wear a hat.
We jumped into the *freezing* water of Lake Superior.
My hands are *freezing*.

senses.gloss: Feeling very cold, of a person.
examples: Can you close the window? I'm *freezing*.
The kids came in from the snow *freezing* and hungry.

senses.gloss: At or below 32°F (0°C), the temperature at which water turns to ice.
examples: *Freezing* temperatures are expected in Atlanta tonight.
Drive carefully — there's *freezing* rain on the roads.

position: both — the heat sense usually after *be* (*It's boiling in here*); the sense of water or oil at boiling point only before a noun (*boiling water*)
comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely boiling*, not *very boiling*
contrast: Extreme, so not *very boiling*. *Boiling water* is still bubbling (Russian *кипяток*); *boiled water* has been boiled and may have cooled (*кипячёная вода*), and a *boiled egg* is cooked. In *boiling hot* and *boiling mad* the word works like an adverb meaning *extremely*.

senses.gloss: Extremely hot, of the weather, a place or a person, informal.
examples: It's *boiling* in here — can we turn on the AC?
I was *boiling* in that wool sweater.
We waited two hours on a *boiling* sidewalk in Phoenix.

senses.gloss: Heated to the point where it bubbles and turns to steam.
examples: Drop the pasta into *boiling* water.
Pour the *boiling* water over the tea bags and wait three minutes.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely starving*, not *very starving*
takes: *for* + noun — wanting something badly (*starving for attention*)
contrast: *I'm starving* is everyday American for *I'm very hungry*, and nobody takes it literally. It is extreme, so not *very starving*: say *I'm starving* or *I'm so hungry*. For sense 3 the past participle is at least as common: *starved for attention*.

senses.gloss: Very hungry, informal.
examples: What's for dinner? I'm *starving*.
The kids were *starving* after soccer practice.

senses.gloss: Suffering or dying because there is not enough food.
examples: The charity sends food to *starving* families in the region.
Rescuers found the dogs cold and *starving*.

senses.gloss: Wanting something very much because you have not had enough of it.
examples: Small towns are *starving* for good jobs.
He was *starving* for someone to talk to.

comparison: more/most — *more furious*, *most furious*; extreme, so *absolutely furious* rather than *very furious*
takes: *at* or *with* a person; *about*, *over* or *at* a thing; *that*-clause
contrast: *Furious* already means *very angry*, so say *absolutely furious* or *really furious*, not *very furious*. The prepositions follow *angry*: *furious at* or *with* someone, *furious about* or *over* something. Sense 2 has nothing to do with anger — *a furious pace* is simply a very fast one.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry.
examples: My dad was *furious* when he saw the dent in the car.
She's *furious* with her brother for telling everyone.
Voters grew *more furious* about the tax increase every week.

senses.gloss: Very fast, energetic or violent.
examples: The workers kept up a *furious* pace all week.
The storm hit the coast with *furious* force.
A *furious* debate broke out online.

comparison: more/most — *more delicious*, *most delicious*; extreme, so *absolutely delicious* rather than *very delicious*
contrast: *Delicious* is much stronger than *tasty* or *good*. Because it already means *very tasty*, *really delicious* and *absolutely delicious* sound natural and *very delicious* sounds like a learner.

senses.gloss: Having a very pleasant taste or smell.
examples: Thanks for dinner — the lasagna was *delicious*.
A *delicious* smell was coming from the kitchen.
That's the *most delicious* pie I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant or enjoyable.
examples: There was a *delicious* irony in losing to his old team.
She had a *delicious* secret she couldn't wait to share.

comparison: more/most — *more hilarious*, *most hilarious*; extreme, so *absolutely hilarious*, not *very hilarious*
contrast: *Hilarious* means *extremely funny*, so *very hilarious* is wrong — say *really hilarious* or *absolutely hilarious*, or just *very funny*. It describes what makes people laugh, not how a person feels: *The movie was hilarious*, not *I felt hilarious*.

senses.gloss: Extremely funny.
examples: Her impression of our boss was *hilarious*.
We watched a *hilarious* video of a cat stealing a taco.
It was the *most hilarious* thing I'd seen all year.

position: both — the 'very great' sense only before a noun (*an awful lot*)
comparison: more/most — *more awful*, *most awful*; *really awful* or *absolutely awful* rather than *very awful*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* — guilty or sorry (*feel awful about it*); *to* a person — unkind (*awful to her*); *that*-clause after *it* (*It's awful that he lost his job*)
contrast: *Awful* and *awesome* both come from *awe* but now mean opposite things: *awful* is very bad, *awesome* is great. Americans also use *awful* as an adverb in speech (*awful tired*, *awful nice*); that is informal — in writing use *awfully* or *really*. *An awful lot* just means a very large amount and is not negative. Spelling: *awful*, never *aweful*.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant.
examples: The traffic on I-95 was *awful* this morning.
He was *awful* to his little sister.
It was the *most awful* week of my life.

senses.gloss: Ill; not well.
examples: I feel *awful* — I think I'm getting the flu.
You look *awful*. Go home and rest.

senses.gloss: Guilty or sorry about something.
examples: I feel *awful* about forgetting your birthday.
She felt *awful* that she couldn't help.

senses.gloss: Very great in amount or degree, used for emphasis before a noun.
examples: That's an *awful* lot of money for a used car.
He's gone to an *awful* lot of trouble for us.

comparison: more/most — *more terrible*, *most terrible*; *really terrible* rather than *very terrible*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* — bad at doing something (*terrible at math*); *about* — guilty or sorry (*feel terrible about it*); *to* a person — unkind
contrast: The adverb *terribly* usually just means *very* and is not negative (*terribly sorry*, *terribly important*). Don't confuse *terrible* with *terrific*, which in American English means *great* (*You did a terrific job*), even though it looks related to *terror*. For skill use *at*: *I'm terrible at math*, not *in math*.

senses.gloss: Very bad, unpleasant or serious; causing great harm, pain or fear.
examples: There was a *terrible* accident on the highway last night.
The food at that place is *terrible*.
It was the *most terrible* storm the town had ever seen.

senses.gloss: Very bad at doing something; lacking skill.
examples: I'm *terrible* at remembering names.
He's a *terrible* driver.

senses.gloss: Ill; not well.
examples: I feel *terrible* — I didn't sleep at all.
She looked *terrible* after the long flight.

senses.gloss: Guilty or sorry about something.
examples: I feel *terrible* about what I said to you.
He felt *terrible* that he'd missed her game.

comparison: not gradable — extreme in the 'excellent' sense: *absolutely fantastic*, not *very fantastic*
contrast: False friend: Russian *фантастика* is *science fiction* or *fantasy* — a sci-fi book is *a science fiction novel*, while *a fantastic novel* is just a wonderful one. In everyday American English *fantastic* almost always means *excellent*; sense 3 belongs to books, art and ideas. Extreme, so *absolutely fantastic*, not *very fantastic*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good; wonderful.
examples: You look *fantastic*!
We had a *fantastic* time in New Orleans.
Your presentation was *fantastic*.

senses.gloss: Extremely large, of an amount.
examples: Some players earn *fantastic* sums of money.
The company grew at a *fantastic* rate.

senses.gloss: Strange and imaginative, or too strange to be believed.
examples: The book is full of *fantastic* creatures and talking animals.
He told some *fantastic* story about being chased by a bear.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely excellent* or *truly excellent*, not *very excellent*; *most excellent* is a joke or a formal title
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* — very good at (*excellent at chess*); *for* — very well suited to (*excellent for beginners*)
contrast: *Excellent* is already the top of *good*, so *very excellent* and *more excellent* are learner errors; to rank two excellent things, say one is *even better*. *Excellent!* on its own is a reply meaning *great*. Spelling: double *l* and *-ent*, not *-ant*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good; of very high quality.
examples: She speaks *excellent* Spanish.
The service at the hotel was *excellent*.
This park is *excellent* for little kids.

comparison: more/most — *more gorgeous*, *most gorgeous*; extreme, so *absolutely gorgeous* rather than *very gorgeous*
contrast: *Gorgeous* is much stronger than *pretty* and is used for men as well as women (*a gorgeous guy*). Americans use it just as freely for weather, places and food, where it means *wonderful*. Extreme, so *absolutely gorgeous* or *so gorgeous*, not *very gorgeous*.

senses.gloss: Very beautiful or attractive.
examples: The bride looked *gorgeous*.
They have a *gorgeous* view of the bay.
She's the *most gorgeous* baby I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant, of the weather, food or an experience.
examples: It's a *gorgeous* day — let's eat outside.
The weather in San Diego was *gorgeous* all week.

comparison: -er/-est — *filthier*, *filthiest*
contrast: *Filthy* is the extreme of *dirty*, so *absolutely filthy*, not *very filthy*. In *filthy rich* it works as an adverb meaning *extremely* and says nothing about dirt. For jokes and language the neutral word is *dirty* (*a dirty joke*); *filthy* is much stronger.

senses.gloss: Extremely dirty.
examples: Take off those *filthy* boots before you come in.
The bathroom at the gas station was *filthy*.
It was the *filthiest* kitchen the inspector had ever seen.

senses.gloss: Obscene or offensive, of words, jokes or pictures.
examples: His mom told him to stop using such *filthy* language.
The comedian's jokes got *filthier* as the night went on.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant or morally disgusting.
examples: Smoking is a *filthy* habit.
Get out of my house, you *filthy* liar!

comparison: not gradable — absolute: *completely spotless*, *absolutely spotless*, not *very spotless*
contrast: Absolute, so *very spotless* is wrong — say *spotless* or *spotlessly clean*. Sense 2 goes mostly with *record* and *reputation*: *a spotless driving record* means no tickets and no accidents.

senses.gloss: Perfectly clean.
examples: Her kitchen is always *spotless*.
He wore a *spotless* white shirt to the interview.
The hotel room was *spotless*.

senses.gloss: Without any fault or bad mark.
examples: She has a *spotless* driving record.
The senator's reputation was *spotless* until the scandal.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun (*ancient Rome*)
comparison: more/most — *more ancient*, *most ancient*
contrast: False friend: Russian *античный* is English *ancient* or *classical* (*ancient Greece*, *classical art*), while English *antique* means old and valuable, like furniture (*антикварный*). *Ancient* is not the everyday word for an old person — *old* or *elderly* is; calling someone *ancient* is a joke or an insult.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the very distant past, especially to the civilizations before the fall of Rome.
examples: We studied *ancient* Greece and Rome in sixth grade.
The museum has a room full of *ancient* Egyptian jewelry.

senses.gloss: Having existed for a very long time.
examples: The town is built around an *ancient* oak tree.
These are some of the *most ancient* rocks on Earth.
The custom is *ancient*.

senses.gloss: Very old or old-fashioned, humorous.
examples: My laptop is *ancient* — it takes five minutes to start.
Don't ask him about TikTok; he's *ancient*.

position: both — sense 3 only after a verb (*I'm all packed*)
comparison: not gradable — extreme: *completely packed*, *absolutely packed* or *jam-packed*, not *very packed*
takes: *with* + noun — full of (*packed with tourists*, *packed with vitamins*)
contrast: *Packed* already means *very crowded*, so *very packed* sounds wrong; Americans say *packed*, *jam-packed* or *completely packed*. *Are you packed?* asks whether someone has finished packing a suitcase, not whether they are in a crowd. Don't confuse it with *packaged* (*packaged food*, sold in a package).

senses.gloss: Extremely crowded.
examples: The subway was *packed* at 8 a.m.
The band played to a *packed* stadium.
The restaurant is always *packed* on Fridays.

senses.gloss: Containing a lot of something.
examples: The guidebook is *packed* with useful tips.
The movie is *packed* with action from start to finish.

senses.gloss: Having finished putting your things into bags for a trip.
examples: Are you *packed* yet? The cab's coming at six.
I'm all *packed* and ready to go.

senses.gloss: Pressed down hard, of snow, soil or earth.
examples: Cars kept sliding on the *packed* snow.
The trail was *packed* dirt, hard as concrete.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *completely soaked*, *soaked through*, not *very soaked*
takes: *through* or *to the skin* — completely wet; *in* or *with* a liquid or a quality (*soaked in sweat*, *soaked in history*)
contrast: *Soaked* is the extreme of *wet*, so not *very soaked*: say *soaked*, *soaked through* or *soaking wet*. In *soaking wet* the *-ing* form works like an adverb meaning *completely*. Before a noun it often forms a hyphenated compound: *a blood-soaked shirt*, *a rain-soaked field*.

senses.gloss: Completely wet.
examples: We got caught in the storm and came home *soaked*.
Take off those *soaked* socks.
His shirt was *soaked* through with sweat.

senses.gloss: Full of a quality or feeling, literary.
examples: The film is *soaked* in nostalgia for the 1980s.
Boston is a city *soaked* in history.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely devastated*, *completely devastated*, not *very devastated*
takes: *by* or *at* + noun — the cause (*devastated by the news*); *to*-infinitive (*devastated to learn*); *that*-clause
contrast: *-ed/-ing* pair: the person is *devastated*; the news, loss or storm is *devastating*. *Devastated* means shocked and deeply hurt, far stronger than *disappointed* or *sad* — used about losing a game it is an exaggeration. Extreme, so not *very devastated*.

senses.gloss: Extremely shocked and upset.
examples: She was *devastated* by her father's death.
The players were *devastated* to lose in the final seconds.
Fans were *devastated* that the show was canceled.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged or destroyed, of a place.
examples: Volunteers brought water to the *devastated* town.
After the hurricane, the whole coast looked *devastated*.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely ecstatic*, not *very ecstatic*
takes: *about*, *over* or *at* + noun; *to*-infinitive; *that*-clause
contrast: Russian *экстатический* suggests a trance or religious rapture; everyday American *ecstatic* just means *thrilled*: *I'm ecstatic about the new job*. Extreme, so *absolutely ecstatic* rather than *very ecstatic*.

senses.gloss: Extremely happy and excited.
senses.ru: в восторге, вне себя от радости
examples: My parents were *ecstatic* when I got into college.
She was *ecstatic* about the promotion.
Fans were *ecstatic* to see the band back together.

senses.gloss: Relating to a state of intense religious or spiritual feeling, like a trance.
examples: The saint wrote about his *ecstatic* visions.
The dancers moved in an *ecstatic* trance.

position: both — the fear sense mostly after *be*; before a noun it usually means turned to stone (*petrified wood*)
comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely petrified*, not *very petrified*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing*; *to*-infinitive; *that*-clause
contrast: *Petrified* is the extreme of *scared* — so frightened you cannot move — so *very petrified* is wrong. The person is *petrified*; the experience is *petrifying* or *terrifying*.

senses.gloss: Extremely frightened, often too frightened to move.
examples: I'm *petrified* of snakes.
She was *petrified* to walk home alone after dark.
He stood there, *petrified*, as the bear came closer.

senses.gloss: Turned slowly into stone over a very long time.
examples: Arizona's *Petrified* Forest is full of ancient logs turned to stone.
The kids found a piece of *petrified* wood near the river.

position: both — the 'complete, exact' sense only before a noun (*dead silence*)
comparison: not gradable — absolute: *completely dead*, *almost dead*; *deader* appears only in jokes
contrast: *Dead* is the adjective, *died* the past of the verb, *death* the noun: *He is dead* or *He died last year*, never *He is died*. Something that kills is *deadly*, not *dead* (*a deadly disease*). As an adverb *dead* means *completely* or *exactly* — *dead tired*, *dead serious*, *dead ahead* — and has nothing to do with death. For a leg or foot that has lost feeling Americans more often say it *fell asleep*.

senses.gloss: No longer alive.
examples: Her grandfather has been *dead* for ten years.
We found a *dead* bird on the porch.
Water the plants or they'll be *dead* by Friday.

senses.gloss: Not working, especially because there is no power.
examples: My phone's *dead* — can I borrow your charger?
The car wouldn't start because the battery was *dead*.
The line suddenly went *dead*.

senses.gloss: Very quiet, with no activity, energy or feeling.
examples: Downtown is *dead* after six o'clock.
Business has been *dead* all week.
He answered in a flat, *dead* voice.

senses.gloss: No longer used, active or likely to happen.
examples: Latin is a *dead* language.
After the vote, the bill is *dead*.

senses.gloss: Unable to feel anything, of a part of the body.
examples: I slept on my arm, and now it's completely *dead*.
My legs went *dead* from sitting on the floor.

senses.gloss: Complete or exact, used before a noun.
examples: There was *dead* silence in the courtroom.
The arrow hit the *dead* center of the target.
The train came to a *dead* stop.

senses.gloss: In serious trouble, informal.
examples: If Mom sees this mess, we're *dead*.
You're *dead* when Coach finds out.

senses.gloss: Extremely tired, informal.
examples: After the double shift I was *dead*.
We were *dead* on our feet by the time the movers left.

comparison: not gradable — absolute in careful use: *completely unique*, *almost unique*; *very unique* and *more unique* are common in speech in sense 2, but editors and exams mark them wrong
takes: *to* + noun — found only in or with (*unique to Hawaii*)
contrast: *Unique* begins with a *y* sound, so it takes *a*: *a unique chance*, not *an unique chance*. In careful writing it means *the only one of its kind*, which cannot be more or less true, so *very unique* and *rather unique* are marked as errors; when you mean *special*, say *unusual*, *rare* or *distinctive*.

senses.gloss: Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
examples: Every snowflake is *unique*.
Each user gets a *unique* password.
This is a *unique* opportunity to work with NASA scientists.

senses.gloss: Unusual or special, informal.
examples: The restaurant has a really *unique* atmosphere.
Her sense of style is pretty *unique*.

senses.gloss: Belonging only to one particular person, place, group or thing.
examples: These birds are *unique* to the Galápagos Islands.
The problem isn't *unique* to our school.

position: both — senses 3 and 4 only before a noun (*a perfect stranger*, *the perfect tenses*)
comparison: not gradable — absolute in careful use: *absolutely perfect*, *almost perfect*; *more perfect* has a long history (*a more perfect Union*, in the U.S. Constitution)
takes: *for* + noun or *-ing* — exactly right for (*perfect for a picnic*)
contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable (PUR-fikt); the verb *to perfect* is stressed on the second (pur-FEKT). *Perfect* already means *as good as possible*, so *very perfect* is wrong; *almost perfect* and *absolutely perfect* are fine. In *a perfect stranger* and *perfect sense* it only adds emphasis — a *perfect stranger* is someone you have never met, not an ideal one.

senses.gloss: Having no mistakes or faults; as good as it can be.
examples: She got a *perfect* score on the SAT.
Nobody's *perfect*.
It was a *perfect* fall day.

senses.gloss: Exactly right for a particular person, purpose or situation.
examples: This dress is *perfect* for the wedding.
You'd be *perfect* for the job.
Six o'clock? That's *perfect* — thanks!

senses.gloss: Complete, used for emphasis before a noun.
examples: I told my life story to a *perfect* stranger on the plane.
What he said makes *perfect* sense.

senses.gloss: In grammar, describing a verb tense made with a form of *have* and a past participle, which shows a completed action.
examples: English has three *perfect* tenses: past, present and future.
In *perfect* verb forms the helping verb is always a form of have.

comparison: not gradable — absolute: *completely impossible*, *almost impossible*, *nearly impossible*, not *very impossible*
takes: *to*-infinitive (*impossible to find*); *for* someone + *to*-infinitive (*impossible for me to leave*); *that*-clause after *it* (*It's impossible that she knew*)
contrast: The situation, not the person, is impossible: *It's impossible for me to come*, not *I am impossible to come*. A person can be the subject only when the infinitive is about dealing with them (*He's impossible to talk to*), or on its own in sense 2 (*My brother is impossible*). *Almost* and *nearly impossible* are the natural way to soften it; *very impossible* is wrong.

senses.gloss: Not able to happen, exist or be done.
examples: It's *impossible* to find parking downtown on Saturdays.
Finishing the whole report by Friday is *impossible*.
The snow made travel almost *impossible*.

senses.gloss: Very difficult to deal with or bear, of a person or situation.
examples: The kids have been *impossible* all day.
Her boss put her in an *impossible* position.

position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun; sense 3 only in *essential oil*
comparison: not gradable — *absolutely essential*, not *very essential*; *most essential* is common in speech in the sense 'most basic'
takes: *to* or *for* + noun (*essential to success*, *essential for growth*); *to*-infinitive after *it* (*It's essential to book early*); *that*-clause, often with the base form of the verb (*It's essential that he be there*)
contrast: *Essential* is much stronger than *important*: it means you cannot do without it. After *It is essential that*, formal American English uses the base verb: *It's essential that every student attend*, not *attends*. *Essential oil* is Russian *эфирное масло*, and *the essentials* (a noun) are the basic things you need.

senses.gloss: Completely necessary.
examples: Water is *essential* for life.
*Essential* workers like nurses and grocery clerks kept working through the pandemic.
It's *essential* that you bring your passport.

senses.gloss: Basic and most important; forming the central part of something.
examples: The *essential* difference between the two plans is cost.
Honesty is an *essential* part of her character.

senses.gloss: Taken from a plant and carrying its smell or flavor, of an oil.
examples: She adds a few drops of lavender *essential* oil to her bath.
*Essential* oils should never be swallowed.

comparison: not gradable — absolute: *six months pregnant*; *very pregnant* is a joke meaning late in pregnancy and clearly showing
takes: *with* a baby (*pregnant with twins*); *by* the father; *with* meaning or feeling, literary (sense 2)
contrast: Say *She is pregnant* or *She is expecting*, not *She is in pregnancy*; for becoming pregnant Americans say *get pregnant*. The length of time goes before the adjective: *She's seven months pregnant*. Absolute, so *very pregnant* is only a joke.

senses.gloss: Carrying a developing baby inside the body.
examples: My sister is *pregnant* with twins.
*Pregnant* women should check with a doctor before taking any medicine.
She got *pregnant* right after the wedding.

senses.gloss: Full of meaning or unspoken feeling.
examples: There was a *pregnant* pause before she answered.
His silence was *pregnant* with meaning.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun (*married life*)
comparison: not gradable — absolute: *happily married*, *newly married*, not *more married*
takes: *to* a person — never *with* or *on* (*married to a doctor*); *to* a job or an idea — devoted to it
contrast: Use *to*: *She's married to a teacher*, not *with* or *on* (Russian *замужем за*, *женат на*). *Married with children* is a different pattern — married and having children. *Be married* is the state and *get married* the event: *We got married in 2019* and *We've been married for five years*, not *We are married for five years*. English has one word for both *женат* and *замужем*.

senses.gloss: Having a husband or wife.
examples: Are you *married*?
They've been *married* for thirty years.
A young *married* couple lives next door.

senses.gloss: Relating to marriage or to a husband and wife.
examples: They were still getting used to *married* life.
She kept her *married* name after the divorce.

senses.gloss: Completely devoted to something and unwilling to give it up.
examples: He's *married* to his job.
The mayor isn't *married* to the plan; she's open to changes.

comparison: not gradable — absolute in the 'right' sense, but *more correct* and *most correct* are common when comparing how accurate something is (*the most correct answer*)
takes: *in* + *-ing* — right to think so (*correct in assuming*); *to*-infinitive (*You were correct to call*)
contrast: False friend: Russian *корректный* usually means *polite* or *tactful* — in English say *polite*, *courteous* or *respectful*. English *correct* behavior means following the accepted rules, as in *politically correct*. *You're correct* is more formal than *You're right*. The verb *correct* (to fix mistakes) looks and sounds the same.

senses.gloss: Right or true; without mistakes.
examples: Is this the *correct* address?
Your answer is *correct*.
Choose the *most correct* answer from the list.

senses.gloss: Right in what you think or say, of a person.
examples: You're absolutely *correct*.
Am I *correct* in thinking you two have met?

senses.gloss: Following the accepted rules of behavior or of a situation.
examples: What's the *correct* way to address a senator?
His manners were always *correct* but cold.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun (*a complete stranger*); *complete with* follows its noun
comparison: not gradable — absolute when it means finished, but *more complete* and *most complete* are normal for having more of the parts (*a more complete list*)
takes: *with* + noun — including something extra (*a kitchen complete with dishwasher*)
contrast: *Complete* is both an adjective and a verb: *The work is complete* (done) and *They completed the work*. A *completed* form is one someone has filled out. In *a complete idiot* or *complete nonsense* it only adds emphasis, like *total*. *Complete with* is a description pattern that comes after the noun: *a house complete with a pool*.

senses.gloss: Having all the parts it should have; whole.
examples: We finally have a *complete* set of the Harry Potter books.
The list isn't *complete* — we're missing three names.
This is the *most complete* collection of her letters.

senses.gloss: Finished.
examples: Work on the new bridge is almost *complete*.
Your registration is not *complete* until you pay the fee.

senses.gloss: Total, used for emphasis before a noun.
examples: The meeting was a *complete* waste of time.
I felt like a *complete* idiot.
She's a *complete* stranger to me.

senses.gloss: Including something as an extra part, after a noun.
examples: The apartment comes *complete* with a washer and dryer.
He showed up dressed as Santa, *complete* with a white beard.

position: attributive only — in both senses; after *be* only in formal writing about sense 2 (*The destruction was total*)
comparison: not gradable — absolute
contrast: *Total* goes before its noun: *The total cost is $50*, not *The cost is total $50*. After a verb Americans use the noun or the verb: *The total is $50*, *The bill totals $50*. In informal American English the verb *total* also means to wreck a car completely: *He totaled his car* (one *l*). The adverb *totally* in speech often just means *completely* or *yes*: *I totally agree*.

senses.gloss: Including everything; being the whole amount.
examples: The *total* cost of the trip was about $3,000.
What's the *total* number of students in the program?

senses.gloss: Complete, used for emphasis.
examples: The party was a *total* disaster.
There was *total* silence in the room.
I felt like a *total* fool.

comparison: -er/-est — *emptier*, *emptiest*
takes: *of* + noun — formal, without (*streets empty of cars*)
contrast: Russian *пустой* covers more than English *empty*. A page or form with nothing written on it is *blank*; a seat nobody is using is *free* (*Is this seat taken?*); an apartment or a job with nobody in it is *vacant*. *Empty* is also a verb (*empty the dishwasher*). Although it sounds absolute, *almost empty*, *emptier* and *emptiest* are all normal.

senses.gloss: Containing nothing, or with no people in it.
examples: The fridge is *empty* — we need to go shopping.
We walked through the *empty* streets at dawn.
The stadium was *emptier* than usual for a playoff game.

senses.gloss: Without meaning, value or real intention.
examples: Voters are tired of *empty* promises.
His threats turned out to be *empty*.

senses.gloss: Feeling that life has no meaning or purpose, of a person.
examples: She felt *empty* for months after the divorce.
Winning didn't make him happy; he just felt *empty*.

position: both — with *of* it can follow the noun (*a room full of people*)
comparison: -er/-est — *fuller*, *fullest*
takes: *of* + noun — containing a lot (*full of water*, *full of ideas*); *of* oneself — too proud
contrast: False friend: Russian *полный* about a person often means *overweight*, but English *I'm full* means *I'm not hungry any more*: *No dessert, thanks — I'm full*. For weight say *heavy* or *overweight*; *a fuller figure* is only a polite fashion phrase. *Full of* follows its noun naturally: *a box full of toys*. The suffix *-ful* has one *l*: *careful*, *spoonful*. *To the fullest* means *as much as possible* (*live life to the fullest*).

senses.gloss: Containing as much or as many as it can hold, or a lot of something.
examples: The parking lot was *full*, so we parked on the street.
She handed me a glass *full* of ice water.
The kids were *full* of energy.

senses.gloss: Having eaten enough; not hungry.
examples: I'm *full* — I can't eat another bite.
Eat slowly and you'll feel *full* sooner.

senses.gloss: Complete, whole or as great as possible.
examples: Please write your *full* name.
The train was moving at *full* speed.
We got a *full* refund.

senses.gloss: Busy, with a lot of activities.
examples: I have a really *full* schedule this week.
She lived a long and *full* life.

senses.gloss: Round and large, of the face, lips or body; wide, of clothing.
examples: She has *full* lips and dark eyes.
The dress has a *full* skirt.
The brand makes jeans for a *fuller* figure.

senses.gloss: Rich and strong, of a sound, taste or color.
examples: The wine has a *full*, fruity flavor.
The cello has a *fuller* sound than the viola.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun (*the final chapter*)
comparison: not gradable — absolute
contrast: *Final* and *last* overlap in sense 1, but *final* stresses that nothing comes after: *the final episode*. After *be*, *final* has sense 2: *The decision is final* means it cannot be changed, not that it came last. The adverb *finally* usually means *after a long time* (*She finally called*). *The finals* (a noun) are the last games of a tournament or end-of-term exams.

senses.gloss: Coming at the end; last in a series.
examples: The *final* chapter surprised everyone.
She scored in the *final* minute of the game.
This is your *final* warning.

senses.gloss: Not able to be changed or argued about.
examples: The judge's decision is *final*.
Is that your *final* answer?

comparison: not gradable — absolute: *almost universal*, *nearly universal*; *more universal* occurs, meaning more widespread
contrast: Russian *универсальный* often means *versatile* — for a person or tool that can do many things say *versatile* or *all-purpose* (*a versatile actor*, *an all-purpose cleaner*), not *universal*. English *universal* means *for everyone* or *everywhere*; the 'fits everything' sense lives in a few set phrases: *universal remote*, *universal adapter*.

senses.gloss: Involving or done by everyone in a group or in the world.
examples: The plan has *universal* support among the teachers.
Canada has *universal* health care.
Cell phone ownership is now nearly *universal*.

senses.gloss: True or found everywhere and in every case.
examples: Music is a *universal* language.
The love of parents for their children is *universal*.

senses.gloss: Able to be used with all or most types of something, of a device.
examples: I lost the *universal* remote again.
Pack a *universal* adapter for the trip.

comparison: not gradable — absolute; to compare, use the adverb: *infinitely better*
contrast: Pronunciation trap: *finite* is FY-nyt, but *infinite* is IN-fuh-nuht — the stress moves and both vowels change. Don't confuse it with the grammar term *infinitive* (*to go*). *Infinite* is absolute, so *very infinite* is wrong; to compare use *infinitely* (*infinitely more complicated*).

senses.gloss: Without limits or an end.
examples: Is the universe *infinite*?
There are an *infinite* number of points on a line.
The set of whole numbers is *infinite*.

senses.gloss: Very great, as if without limit.
examples: The teacher showed *infinite* patience with the class.
She wrapped the old photos with *infinite* care.

comparison: not gradable — absolute; *more equal* is a famous joke from Orwell's *Animal Farm* (*some animals are more equal than others*)
takes: *to* + noun — the same as (*equal to one mile*); *to* a task — able to do it; *in* + noun — the way they are the same (*equal in size*)
contrast: Use *equal to*, not *equal with*, for amounts: *One yard is equal to three feet*. In math Americans usually use the verb: *Two plus two equals four*. *Equal* is about size, value or rights; for things that are exactly alike use *the same*: *We have the same car*, not *equal cars*. As a noun, *an equal* is a person of the same rank (*She treated us as equals*).

senses.gloss: The same in size, amount, number or value.
examples: Cut the cake into eight *equal* pieces.
One kilometer is *equal* to about 0.62 miles.
The two bedrooms are *equal* in size.

senses.gloss: Having the same rights, status or opportunities.
examples: The Declaration of Independence says that all men are created *equal*.
Women are still fighting for *equal* pay.
They're *equal* partners in the business.

senses.gloss: Having the ability or strength to deal with something.
examples: She proved *equal* to the challenge.
I wasn't sure he was *equal* to the job.
